en: Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, the essence is to be taken from three things that lack essence. From which three? From the body, from wealth, and from life."

[1] How is the essence to be taken from this essenceless body? Here, a son of good family becomes one who performs the acts of salutation, prostration, rising to greet, joining the palms, and respectful conduct toward those worthy of such acts. In this way, the essence is to be taken from this essenceless body.

[2] How is the essence to be extracted from insubstantial enjoyments? In this case, a son of good family becomes a giver of gifts to ascetics, brahmins, the wretched, beggars, travelers, and supplicants. That is to say: food, drink, edibles, delicacies, vehicles, clothing, garlands, perfumes, ointments, shelter, and the gift of lamps. In this way, the essence is to be extracted from insubstantial enjoyments.

[3] How is the essence to be taken from this essenceless life? Here, noble son, one understands as it truly is: "This is the noble truth of suffering"; one understands as it truly is: "This is the origin of suffering," "This is the cessation of suffering," and "This is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. In this way, the essence is to be taken from this essenceless life. [4] The Blessed One said this; having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke these words:
Those possessed of wisdom, who delight in the word of the Victor, take up that [practice] which concerns the body, enjoyments, and life. (1)
Those great sages who always follow the Dharma and honor the virtuous men have attained the essence of life, being disciplined in the word of the Conqueror.
Those who are devoted to the word of the Victor and offer gifts to the Saṅgha—
by them are gains obtained here, and their human existence has become fruitful.
